clue.text: Young bird's broken home

parts.note: a chick's home before hatching is the shell it lives in, left broken once it emerges

explanation.surface: A sad tale of a fledgling from a broken family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken home' suggests family breakdown; read literally it is the cracked shell a chick leaves behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The shell around a chick is its first dwelling, and hatching breaks it.

clue.text: Deprived of shelter, sounded cross and puzzled

indicators.note: sounded means the letter is written as it is said

parts.note: a cross is the letter X
posed, as of a problem, means puzzled or set a puzzle

explanation.surface: Someone left out in the cold, voicing anger and confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounded cross' looks like 'spoke angrily'; it is the letter X said aloud, EX.
explanation.definitionFit: Left unprotected, open to wind and weather, is the state of having no cover.

clue.text: Not the horsy chap's servant, though he may hold the ring

definitions.text: Not the horsy chap's servant, though he may hold the ring

parts.words: Not the horsy chap's servant, though he may hold the ring
parts.note: the stable-hand's assistant is a false lead; the man meant attends a bridegroom and may keep the wedding ring

explanation.surface: A man who is no stable lad's helper, yet may be trusted with a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: A groom also looks after horses, so a 'groom's man' could be his servant; the wedding sense is the real one.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridegroom's attendant at a wedding, sometimes the best man holding the ring.

clue.text: Spanish gent's concealed gaol break

parts.note: concealed means hid

indicators.note: a gaol break smashes out of prison, so the letters of the prison word are broken up

explanation.surface: A Spanish nobleman's secret prison escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaol break' reads as an escape; 'break' is the anagram signal on GAOL, giving ALGO.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidalgo is a member of the minor Spanish nobility, a gentleman.

clue.text: Pulses pound — listen out

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the hearing word are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A pulse is pounding: listen out for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulses' looks like heartbeats, which fits 'pound' and 'listen'; it means edible seeds.
explanation.definitionFit: Lentils are edible seeds of a legume, one of the pulses.

clue.text: Plump one married to a Bluebeard

definitions.text: Plump one married to a Bluebeard

parts.note: plump means fat
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A stout woman wed to a murderous husband.
explanation.walkthrough: In Perrault's tale the last wife of Bluebeard, who discovers the bodies of his earlier wives, is called Fatima in many English versions.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatima is the name of the wife in the Bluebeard fairy story.

clue.text: Lighter than a feather when ringed

definitions.text: Lighter than a feather when ringed

parts.words: Lighter than a feather when ringed
parts.note: in boxing, the ring, one weight class sits below the featherweight division

explanation.surface: Something so light it outweighs not even a feather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringed' means in the boxing ring, where weight divisions are named, among others, fly and feather.
explanation.definitionFit: In boxing the fly division is a lower weight class than the feather division.

clue.text: Trooped out, being expelled from tube

indicators.note: out signals the marching word's letters are turned out of order

explanation.surface: Soldiers filed out, as if forced from an Underground carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'tube' is a submarine's launching tube, not the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is the missile fired from a warship's launch tube.

clue.text: Between husband and wife, if it turned warlike

indicators.note: turned asks for the word for warlike to be rearranged; in fact just its I and T swap places

parts.note: warlike means martial

explanation.surface: A domestic row that would become a war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If it turned' hints that only IT is flipped: MARTIAL becomes MAR-IT-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Marital means relating to marriage, the bond between spouses.

clue.text: Slowly trudge to the Dell, missing the end of Mr Winkle

parts.note: to trudge is to plod

indicators.note: missing tells us a letter is taken away from the Dickensian place name

parts.note: Dingley Dell is the country house in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, so the Dell stands for its first word

indicators.note: the end of points to the final letter of the Pickwickian character's surname

explanation.surface: Mr Winkle of Pickwick Papers trudges wearily towards Dingley Dell.
explanation.walkthrough: Nathaniel Winkle is one of the Pickwick Club; his name ends in E, which drops from DINGLEY to leave DINGLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving in a slow, heavy, laborious manner is how a plodder goes.

clue.text: Thin pair of arms

parts.note: RA, the Royal Artillery, is one arm of the British Army
RE, the Royal Engineers, is the other arm of the British Army in the pair

explanation.surface: Someone with two skinny arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' means branches of the army, not limbs: the Royal Artillery (RA) and the Royal Engineers (RE).
explanation.definitionFit: Rare air is thin, of low density, as at altitude.

clue.text: Pure profit from a principal source

definitions.text: Pure profit from a principal source

parts.note: pure means simple, unmixed
interest is the profit earned on money lent or invested

explanation.surface: Unadulterated gain earned from a main origin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' is the banking term for the sum lent; interest calculated on that sum alone, never on earlier interest, has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest reckoned only on the original capital sum, not compounded, is the plain kind.

clue.text: The children are after mother for some fruit

indicators.note: after places the children following the mother in the answer

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, as of a foal
sons are children

explanation.surface: Kids trail behind Mum on a fruit-picking outing.
explanation.definitionFit: Damsons are small purple plums, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: They tell stories when climbing island peaks

indicators.note: climbing, in a down clue, reads the island's name from bottom to top

parts.note: Arran is a Scottish island in the Firth of Clyde
tors are rocky hilltops, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Hikers spin yarns as they scramble up island summits.
explanation.walkthrough: ARRAN is a Scottish island; 'climbing' turns it to NARRA. TORS are craggy hills of south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrators are storytellers who recount events.

clue.text: Base for weaving Gobelin

indicators.note: weaving interlaces strands, so the letters of the tapestry name are worked into a new pattern

explanation.surface: A Gobelin tapestry needs a ground to be woven on.
explanation.walkthrough: Gobelins is the famous Paris tapestry works; 'Base' looks like a noun for the weaving but is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Base in the moral sense means dishonourable, low and mean.

clue.text: Thrace bus re-routed to this capital

indicators.note: a bus re-routed goes a different way, so the letters are sent in a new order

explanation.surface: A Thracian bus is diverted to a Balkan capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Thrace is the Balkan region next to Romania's neighbours, so the surface stays in the area.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucharest is the capital city of Romania.

clue.text: Italian scientist in the tube

explanation.surface: An Italian researcher spotted on the Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: Giovanni Battista Venturi studied fluid flow; a constricted pipe that speeds a fluid is named after him. 'The tube' is not the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Venturi was an eighteenth-century Italian physicist, and his name labels the narrowing pipe used in carburettors and flow meters.

clue.text: Passage from outdated pamphlet

parts.note: ex means former, no longer current
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious

explanation.surface: A section quoted from an old leaflet.
explanation.definitionFit: An extract is a passage taken from a longer text.

clue.text: The wood where this lives is called holy

definitions.text: The wood where this lives is called holy

parts.words: The wood where this lives is called holy
parts.note: holy sounds like holey: an insect boring tunnels leaves its timber full of holes

explanation.surface: A sacred grove where some creature dwells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holy' is to be heard as 'holey'.
explanation.definitionFit: Termites are wood-eating insects that riddle timber with tunnels.

clue.text: Stick to the point, and perhaps press it

parts.note: to stick is to fasten or fix one thing onto another
E is a compass point, east

explanation.surface: Advice to keep to the point and perhaps iron it flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' is not ironing: a press attaché is the embassy official dealing with the media, so 'perhaps press' gives an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A press attaché is one kind of embassy official assigned to a particular field.

clue.text: Someone else still to be selected

explanation.surface: A different person, not yet picked for the team.
explanation.walkthrough: A. N. Other is the placeholder written on British team sheets for a player not yet chosen.
explanation.definitionFit: Another means a different person, and A. N. Other stands for an unnamed squad member yet to be picked.

clue.text: Fixture for which the cavalry make a charge

definitions.text: Fixture for which the cavalry make a charge

parts.words: Fixture for which the cavalry make a charge
parts.note: a mounted sport has horsemen galloping with lances at a camping fastener to lift it from the ground

explanation.surface: A sporting event at which mounted troops attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixture' looks like a sporting date; it is something fixed in the ground. Tent-pegging is a cavalry sport of spearing a peg at a gallop.
explanation.definitionFit: A tent peg holds a guy rope fixed in the ground and is the target in cavalry tent-pegging.

clue.text: How to keep soldiers on the rails?

definitions.text: How to keep soldiers on the rails?

parts.words: How to keep soldiers on the rails?
parts.note: on the rails suggests keeping troops disciplined, but means getting them aboard a railway carriage

explanation.surface: A question about keeping troops in line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rails' reads as 'well behaved'; literally it means on a railway.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrain troops is to load them onto a train.

clue.text: Auditor at Epsom, perhaps? He is certainly a bookman

explanation.surface: An accountant at the races who is also a keen reader.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is an English racecourse, home of the Derby; 'turf' means horse racing. A bookmaker keeps a book of bets, hence 'bookman'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker taking bets on horse races is a racing-world counter of money and a keeper of a betting book.

clue.text: Chronicler of Clovis has a drink, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the drink's name is taken as it is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: sake is Japanese rice wine, a drink

explanation.surface: A historian of the Frankish king takes a tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: Clovis was a Frankish king, but here he is Clovis Sangrail, hero of short stories by H. H. Munro, who wrote as Saki. The printed solution's R is a misread S.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, wrote the Chronicles of Clovis.

clue.text: An order for rare hotpot

indicators.note: for here means arranged in exchange for, the letters of the dish being put into a new order

explanation.surface: A diner asks for the stew to be served underdone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' is the biological rank, the grasshoppers and crickets; the clue also hints that the letters of 'rare hotpot' are put in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Orthoptera is the insect order containing grasshoppers, crickets and locusts.

clue.text: Second pair of trousers covers the surface

parts.note: trews are close-fitting tartan trousers worn in Scotland

explanation.surface: A spare pair of trousers is draped over the table.
explanation.walkthrough: TREWS are Scottish tartan trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: To strew is to scatter things so they lie spread across an area.

clue.text: Drop straight in the swamp and cause alarm

indicators.note: in shows the word for straight is dropped inside the marshland word

parts.note: a fen is low marshy land, a swamp
right means straight, as in a right line

explanation.surface: Someone falls headlong into a bog and raises the alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' tells us to put the word for straight into the swamp. The printed solution's B is a misread F.
explanation.definitionFit: To frighten someone is to scare them, filling them with fear.
